newsitem.title: SPAIN: Basque resort town fearful as violence grows.
newsitem.headline: Basque resort town fearful as violence grows.

text.p: The resort of San Sebastian, famous for its seashell-shaped beach and its prestigious international film festival, has again become a flashpoint of Basque separatist violence and its people are fearful.
When the sun sets, masked Basque policeman with teargas canisters fitted to their rifles fan out on the main boulevard facing the town's old quarter.

They face gangs of violent young supporters of ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) who have succeeded in recreating an atmosphere of intimidation, even though the guerrillas have the full backing of fewer than 15 percent of Basques.

"Underneath what appears to be a beautiful, welcoming city, there is a world of fear...an enormous feeling of vulnerability," said Jose Maria Mugica, a well-known San Sebastian lawyer whose father was killed by ETA last year.

San Sebastian, capital of Guipuzcoa, the most hardline nationalist of the Basque country's three provinces, has always been a hotbed of pro-ETA militancy, but in the past few years street violence had become very sporadic and the clouds of fear had lifted.
But now the pendulum has swung the other way again.
So far this year, ETA has killed six people in Spain, four of them in the past week and a half. The toll has already passed last year's total.
Many say the tension is at its highest point since a 1980s "dirty war" when gun squads began killing and kidnapping suspected ETA activists.
Last month, the government blamed ETA for the killing in San Sebastian of a bicycle merchant who may have been suspected of turning in one of the rebels.

Violent youth groups operate mainly out of the old quarter, where the outer walls of upscale shops are scrawled with pro-ETA graffiti in the Basque language Euskera which only about 30 percent of the region's population speak.
The quarter with its lively bars is the centre of nightlife and thus a magnet for high-school-age supporters of ETA who frequently firebomb buses on the main boulevard just outside it.

With their faces hidden by hoods, the youths strike weekly. Most of the action is on Friday and Saturday nights when the Old Quarter is teeming with people and they can disappear into the crowded narrow streets inside.
The Ertzaintza (Basque police) have taken up a high-profile post along the boulevard recently to try to stem the violence.

Dressed in dark blue uniforms with red shoulder pads and red crash helmets, the police don ski masks with only eyeholes, giving them a sinister look. They do not wear any identifying numbers or nameplates for fear of deadly retaliation by ETA.

"People don't talk about it but they are afraid," said Maria Teresa Castells, a 61-year-old bookshop owner in the Old Quarter whose shop has been vandalised six times in two months by youths supporting ETA.
The vandals have shattered the shop's glass panes and thrown petrol bombs inside which burned some of the books, leaving behind graffiti calling for a liberated Basque homeland.
Castells' Libreria Lagun was once a symbol of free expression under dictator Francisco Franco who ruled until 1975.
She was even jailed for a show of solidarity with ETA under Franco, who repressed any expression of Basque nationalism. Now, Castells says she is an ETA target because she rejects violence.
Others said the violence was becoming an almost "normal" fact of daily life which many try to ignore.
But hundreds of peace activists turned out on Tuesday night in a San Sebastian garden plaza to protest at the killing of a Basque policeman in the nearby city of Bilbao on Monday.
Peace groups hold weekly vigils in the region to demand freedom for two hostages held by ETA and said they are often met by counter-demonstrators threatening and insulting them.
One ETA sympathiser warned of further escalation if the government does not start to grapple with their demands for freedom of ETA prisoners and an independent state in the north.
"When all channels close to defend rights, there are only two ways to go -- resignation or rebellion," he said.
